# Debrief packet: Priya N. -- Senior Backend Engineer (REQ-1042)

As of 2026-10-01. AI-drafted, human decision required. This packet organizes interviewer evidence. It does not score, rank or recommend, and interviewers' overall votes are left out so the discussion starts from evidence.

> Privacy: 2 email/phone/link value(s) were removed from interviewer text.

## 1. Scorecard status

- Submitted: 6 of 7 interviews.
- MISSING: Gabe T. (Debugging & operations, interviewed 2026-09-28) -- 3 day(s) since the interview.
- Late: Chen H. (Technical screen) submitted 2 days after the interview; memory-based notes are less reliable.

## 2. Evidence matrix (competency x interviewer)

| Competency | Interviewer (session) | Rating | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| System Design | Ana Q. (System design) | Yes | "Designed the fleet telemetry ingest for 40k robots: partitioned by robot id, put a durable queue in front of the writer, and named back-pressure and replay as the two failure modes to handle. Picked at-least-once delivery and explained the idempotency key." |
| System Design | Ben O. (System design) | No | "Did not estimate write throughput until I asked; when asked, 40k robots x 10 msgs/s was computed as 40k msgs/s and not corrected. Storage retention was never discussed." |
| System Design | Dev M. (Architecture deep dive) | Strong Yes | "Walked through the billing queue migration in detail: dual writes, a shadow reader, and a rollback switch; quantified the lag budget at 2 seconds." |
| System Design | Farah S. (Architecture deep dive) | No | "The migration story was strong but when I changed the constraint to multi-region she kept a single primary and could not say how a region failover would work." |
| Code Quality & Testing | Chen H. (Technical screen) | Strong Yes | "Solid coder, would be great." |
| Debugging & Operations | -- | -- | NO EVIDENCE |
| Communication | Ana Q. (System design) | Yes | "Drew the design in stages and paused to check that I followed before going deeper; restated my constraint about cost before answering." |
| Communication | Ben O. (System design) | Yes | "Clear structure, explained the queue choice well." |
| Ownership | Elena V. (Hiring manager screen) | Yes | "Described leading the move of the billing queue off a single Postgres table after two incidents; she wrote the RFC, ran the cutover and owned the on-call runbook afterwards." |
| Ownership | Dev M. (Architecture deep dive) | Yes | "Owned the post-incident review and the follow-up work for the billing outage." |
| Ownership | Farah S. (Architecture deep dive) | Yes | "Clear example of owning the billing runbook after the incident." |
| Collaboration | Elena V. (Hiring manager screen) | Yes | "Disagreed with a staff engineer on event schema versioning; set up a short spike to compare both options and adopted his approach when the data favored it." |

## 3. Where interviewers disagree

- **System Design**: 2 positive vs 2 negative.
  - Ana Q. (Yes): "Designed the fleet telemetry ingest for 40k robots: partitioned by robot id, put a durable queue in front of the writer, and named back-pressure and replay as the two failure modes to handle. Picked at-least-once delivery and explained the idempotency key."
  - Dev M. (Strong Yes): "Walked through the billing queue migration in detail: dual writes, a shadow reader, and a rollback switch; quantified the lag budget at 2 seconds."
  - Ben O. (No): "Did not estimate write throughput until I asked; when asked, 40k robots x 10 msgs/s was computed as 40k msgs/s and not corrected. Storage retention was never discussed."
  - Farah S. (No): "The migration story was strong but when I changed the constraint to multi-region she kept a single primary and could not say how a region failover would work."

## 4. Coverage gaps

- **Debugging & Operations**: no evidence. Gabe T. (Debugging & operations) has not submitted.
- Code Quality & Testing: evidence from one interviewer only (Chen H.).
- Collaboration: evidence from one interviewer only (Elena V.).

## 5. Ratings without supporting evidence

- STRONG RATING, THIN EVIDENCE: Chen H. rated Code Quality & Testing "Strong Yes" with 5 word(s) of evidence: "Solid coder, would be great."
- thin evidence: Ben O. rated Communication "Yes" with 7 word(s) of evidence: "Clear structure, explained the queue choice well."
- thin evidence: Farah S. rated Ownership "Yes" with 10 word(s) of evidence: "Clear example of owning the billing runbook after the incident."

## 6. Fairness flags (non-job-related remarks)

- [high] Dev M. (notes): "young" in "Great culture fit -- she brings the young energy this team needs. Email [email removed] if" -- age: Age-coded wording (ADEA protects 40+). Fix: Describe the job-related behaviour instead.
- [medium] Ben O. (notes): "Seemed nervous" in "Seemed nervous at the start, warmed up later." -- demeanor-emotion: Inference about emotion, demeanor or personality. These are unreliable signals, and AI systems may not infer emotions at work (EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)). Fix: Record what the candidate said or did against the rubric.
- [medium] Dev M. (notes): "culture fit" in "Great culture fit -- she brings the young energy this team needs. E" -- culture-fit: 'Culture fit' and gut-feel remarks are not job-related and are a common proxy for similarity bias. Fix: Replace with evidence against a named competency, or with 'values alignment' tied to a written value.

## 7. Questions for the debrief (seeds; edit before use)

1. System Design: Ana Q., Dev M. saw it positively and Ben O., Farah S. negatively. What did each of you observe, and which observation maps to which rubric anchor?
2. Debugging & Operations has no evidence. Do we wait for the missing scorecard, add a follow-up, or decide without it and record that?
3. Chen H.: what specific behaviour supports "Strong Yes" on Code Quality & Testing?
4. Set aside the flagged remarks (Ben O., Dev M.). Is the remaining job-related evidence enough?

## 8. Decision memo (the hiring team fills this in)

- Decision and decider: ______ (made by people, after discussion)
- Evidence relied on, by competency: ______
- Open risks and how they will be checked (references, follow-up interview): ______
- Flagged remarks excluded from the decision: ______
- Missing scorecards and how they were handled: ______

AI-drafted, human decision required.

---

### How the counts and dates were worked out

- **Interviews:** 7 records for Priya N. 6 have a `submitted_at`. Gabe T.'s is `null`.
- **Missing:** Gabe T. interviewed 2026-09-28; as of 2026-10-01, that is 3 days.
- **Late (more than 1 day after the interview):**
  - Chen H.: interviewed 2026-09-15, submitted 2026-09-17, so 2 days (late).
  - Ben O. and Farah S.: interviewed 2026-09-28, submitted 2026-09-29, so 1 day each (not late).
  - Everyone else submitted the same day.
- **Redactions (2):**
  - The phone number `303-555-0147` in Elena V.'s notes.
  - The email address in Dev M.'s notes.
- **Thin evidence (fewer than 12 words):**
  - Chen H.: 5 words.
  - Ben O. (Communication): 7 words.
  - Farah S. (Ownership): 10 words.
  - Dev M. (Ownership): exactly 12 words, so it is not flagged.
- **Disagreement:** System Design is the only competency with both positive ratings (3–4) and negative ratings (1–2).
- **Fairness flags:** Only the notes fields matched a lint rule. No evidence text matched, so nothing in the matrix was excluded.

### Facilitator notes

- **Sharpen the System Design split by asking which constraint each person tested.**
  - Ana Q. tested the stated load of 40k robots: partitioning, back-pressure and replay, and the idempotency key.
  - Dev M. tested a past migration: dual writes, the shadow reader, rollback, and the 2 s lag budget.
  - Ben O. tested capacity arithmetic and retention in the same session as Ana.
  - Farah S. tested a changed constraint, multi-region failover.
  - Questions to ask: "Ana, did you see the 40k × 10 msgs/s calculation that Ben recorded?" and "Farah, was multi-region part of the planned prompt, or did you add it?"
- **Match the evidence to the System Design anchors.**
  - Ana's quote matches anchor 3: the stated load, two failure modes, and trade-offs named.
  - Dev's quote has two parts of anchor 4: a quantified budget and a migration plan. But it describes a past project, not a design produced in the session.
  - Ben's and Farah's quotes match anchor 2: "misses failure modes or capacity limits when prompted."
- **Ask for the missing specifics.**
  - The only Code Quality & Testing evidence is 5 words behind a "Strong Yes". Ask Chen H. to describe the exercise against anchor 4 ("tests drive the design; edge cases covered").
  - Ask Ben O. for the specifics behind the Communication rating.
  - Ask Farah S. for the specifics behind the Ownership rating.
- **Get Gabe T.'s scorecard before the meeting.** It is the only planned source for Debugging & Operations and is 3 days outstanding.
- **Suggested agenda:**
  1. Go through the evidence by competency: System Design first, then the single-source competencies, then the gap.
  2. Exclude the flagged remarks (Dev M.'s and Ben O.'s notes) explicitly, and record that in the memo.
  3. Take votes last.

AI-drafted, human decision required.

**No, don't share it as written.** Four of the five remarks shouldn't go to the panel. The only job-related evidence in it is "skipped error states entirely."

One caveat first. The skill requires running `fairness_lint.py`, but I don't have a shell in this session, so I couldn't run it. Instead I checked the text by hand against the script's rules (`fairness_lint.py:27-84`). Below is what those rules should flag. Please confirm with the actual script before the debrief:

```
cd /home/admin/code/plugin-creator/plugins/structured-hiring/skills/fairness-lint
python3 fairness_lint.py <your-file> --mode feedback
```

**Expected lint result (feedback mode): 5 flags**

| Sev | Line | Category | Phrase | Why | Suggested fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| high | 1 | national-origin | "accent" | National origin, ancestry or language-origin remark. | Assess communication against the rubric (clarity, structure), not accent, language origin or birthplace. |
| high | 3 | family-status | "baby" | Family, marital or pregnancy status is not job-related and is protected in many jurisdictions. | Delete the remark; assess availability only through the job's stated schedule, asked of everyone. |
| medium | 1 | culture-fit | "culture fit" | "Culture fit" and gut-feel remarks are not job-related and are a common proxy for similarity bias. | Replace with evidence against a named competency, or with "values alignment" tied to a written value. |
| medium | 2 | demeanor-emotion | "Seemed nervous" | Inference about emotion, demeanor or personality; unreliable signal. | Record what the candidate said or did against the rubric. |
| medium | 2 | demeanor-emotion | "lacked confidence" | Inference about emotion, demeanor or personality; unreliable signal. | Record what the candidate said or did against the rubric. |

**Reviewer notes (things the patterns can't catch)**
- **"Hard to follow"** could be a real communication point, but it sits right next to "strong accent," so as written it reads as being about the accent. It only counts if it's about structure or clarity, backed by a concrete example.
- **"On-call might be a problem"** is a guess about his availability based on his family. If on-call is part of the role, ask every candidate the same question about the stated schedule.

**Exclude from the decision**
- "strong accent"
- "Not sure he'd be a culture fit with the team"
- "Seemed nervous and lacked confidence"
- "he's got a new baby so on-call might be a problem"

**Questions the interviewer should answer instead**
1. **Communication:** At which point in the design exercise was the explanation hard to follow? Was it the structure, missing steps, or not answering what was asked? Give a specific example.
2. **Design exercise:** What did he cover and what did he miss, against the rubric? "Skipped error states entirely" is a good start. What else was there, good or weak?
3. **Values:** If there's a worry about the team, which written company value does it relate to, and what did he say or do that bears on it?
4. **On-call:** Leave it out of the feedback. If on-call is required, the recruiter should check the schedule requirement with every candidate the same way.

I'd also suggest the interviewer rewrite the feedback in their own words and resubmit it, rather than someone else editing it.

**Cleanup:** I saved your text to `cwd/.fairness_lint_input.txt` to run the script. I couldn't delete it without a shell, so I emptied it. You can delete it.

Flags mean a human should look, not that anyone is biased. AI-drafted, human decision required.

graders.name: flags
graders.evidence:
**No, I wouldn't share it as written.** Parts of it create legal and fairness risk, and most of it isn't evidence about the job. Only one point is solid.

**Remove these:**

- **"Strong accent"**: Accent is closely tied to national origin, which is legally protected in most places. If there was a real communication problem, describe what happened instead. For example: "I had to ask him to clarify his approach to X twice." That's only worth including if clear communication is part of what you're assessing.
- **"New baby so on-call might be a problem"**: This is the most serious one. Family and caregiver status is protected in many jurisdictions, and the conclusion is a guess. It shouldn't appear in written feedback at all. If on-call is a real requirement, everyone gets the same question about it, usually from the recruiter.
- **"Not sure he'd be a culture fit"**: With nothing behind it, this is the phrase that tends to hide bias. Either name a specific behaviour tied to how the team works, or drop it.

**Rework this:**

- **"Seemed nervous and lacked confidence"**: Interview nerves don't tell you much about how someone does the job. Describe what he actually did. Did he change his mind without a reason, need prompting to move forward, or fail to defend his choices when you pushed back?

**Keep this:**

- **"Skipped error states entirely"**: This is specific and observable, and it relates directly to the design exercise.

**Possible rewrite:**

> Design exercise: Jordan produced a reasonable happy-path flow for [X] but didn't address error states (e.g., failed submission, empty/invalid input) and didn't raise them when I asked about edge cases. He needed some prompting to move from initial sketches to a committed approach. [Add any strengths you observed, e.g., how he handled requirements or trade-offs.] Overall: [lean hire / lean no hire] based primarily on the gap in edge-case handling.

If he did well anywhere, add it. Feedback that's only negative reads as less credible to the panel. If the "baby" or "accent" comments have already come up verbally, tell your recruiter or HR partner before the debrief so they can steer the discussion.

graders.evidence:
# Interview kit: Founding Account Executive

You asked me to just draft it, so I assumed a standard loop: a CEO screen, a skills screen and a three-session onsite.

Loop: Hiring manager screen (30 min, CEO) -> Discovery role-play (45 min, Sales advisor) -> Onsite: Pipeline and deal execution (60 min, Sales advisor) | Product and customer feedback (45 min, Head of product) | Building the sales motion (40 min, CEO)

## Panel split
| Session | Interviewer | Owns | Secondary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hiring manager screen | CEO | Learning from deal outcomes | — |
| Discovery role-play | Sales advisor | Discovery and qualification | — |
| Pipeline and deal execution | Sales advisor | Pipeline generation; Deal execution and closing | — |
| Product and customer feedback | Head of product | Product fluency and customer feedback | — |
| Building the sales motion | CEO | Building sales process from zero | — |

Most of the sales craft sits with the advisor because they've seen what good looks like at scale. The CEO tests the part only this first hire faces: turning what you know into a repeatable process.

## Learning from deal outcomes (owned by the hiring manager screen)
Definition: Reviews won and lost deals honestly, finds the real cause, and changes how they sell as a result.
Rubric: 1 Strong No: Blames losses only on price, product or the buyer; can't name anything they changed afterwards. | 2 No: Names a cause, but it's generic ("should have qualified better"); no specific change. | 3 Yes: A specific loss, a cause they own, and a concrete change that showed up in a later deal. | 4 Strong Yes: Does 3, plus regularly reviews outcomes (loss reviews, call reviews, asking buyers why) and can point to a measurable result of a change.
Behavioral
1. Tell me about a deal you lost that you believe you should have won. (10 min)
   Probes: When did you first see it slipping, and what did you do?; What did the buyer tell you about why they chose otherwise?; What do you do differently now because of it?
2. Tell me about a time a manager or peer gave you feedback on your selling that you initially disagreed with. (8 min)
   Probes: What exactly was the feedback?; What did you try as a result?; What happened in the next few deals?
Situational
1. Three months in, you've lost four of your first six late-stage deals, all to "no decision." What do you do in the next two weeks? (7 min)
   Probes: Who would you talk to, and what would you ask?; What data would you pull?; What would you bring to the CEO?

## Discovery and qualification (owned by the discovery role-play)
Definition: Uncovers the buyer's problem, what it costs them, who decides and how they buy, and disqualifies early when there's no real deal.
Rubric: 1 Strong No: Pitches features before understanding the problem; leaves without knowing the pain, the decision maker or the timeline. | 2 No: Asks the standard questions but accepts surface answers; doesn't put a number on the impact or confirm how they buy. | 3 Yes: Gets to a specific problem with a number on it, identifies the decision maker and process, and agrees a concrete next step. | 4 Strong Yes: Does 3, plus surfaces something the buyer hadn't put into words themselves, checks whether the deal could stall with no decision, and would disqualify if the evidence said so.
Situational
1. Mock discovery call. The advisor plays a buyer from a written persona that every candidate gets 48 hours ahead. Run a first discovery call. (30 min: 25 min call, 5 min debrief)
   Probes: Afterwards: Is this a real opportunity, and why?; What don't you know yet that you need to?; What's your next step, and what's it for?
Behavioral
1. Tell me about a deal you walked away from or disqualified early. (7 min)
   Probes: What signals told you?; How did you handle it with the buyer?; What would it have cost you if you hadn't?
2. Tell me about a deal where what the buyer first said they needed turned out to be different from the real problem. (8 min)
   Probes: How did you find out?; What questions got you there?; How did it change the deal?

## Pipeline generation (owned by Pipeline and deal execution)
Definition: Builds their own pipeline from a cold start through targeted outbound, referrals and their network, without relying on marketing leads.
Rubric: 1 Strong No: Has only worked inbound or assigned leads; can't explain how they'd find pipeline themselves. | 2 No: Has done outbound but only talks about volume (emails sent), with no targeting logic or conversion numbers. | 3 Yes: Describes a specific outbound motion they ran: who they targeted and why, the messaging and channels, and rough conversion to meetings and pipeline. | 4 Strong Yes: Does 3, plus changed the motion based on results and found a large share of their closed revenue themselves, with numbers.
Behavioral
1. Walk me through the last time you had to build pipeline mostly on your own. How much of your closed business did you find yourself? (10 min)
   Probes: Who did you target, and why them?; What were your rough numbers from touches to meetings to opportunities?; What did you stop doing because it didn't work?
2. Tell me about an outbound message or sequence that worked noticeably better than your others. (7 min)
   Probes: What was different about it?; How did you know it was better?; Did you ever see it stop working?
Situational
1. Day one here: there are no SDRs and no marketing team, and the CEO's network is mostly used up. You need three times your quarterly quota in pipeline within 90 days. Walk me through your plan. (10 min)
   Probes: Which accounts first, and how do you pick them?; What does your week look like?; What would you measure at day 30 to know it's working?

## Deal execution and closing (owned by Pipeline and deal execution)
Definition: Moves deals with several stakeholders to signature using a close plan agreed with the buyer, handles pricing and procurement, and forecasts accurately.
Rubric: 1 Strong No: Can't describe a close plan beyond "following up"; discounts to close without getting anything back; no sense of how accurate their forecasts have been. | 2 No: Has closed deals but only through a single champion; vague on procurement, legal, or how pricing was negotiated. | 3 Yes: Walks through a specific deal with several stakeholders, a close plan agreed with the buyer, named roles, a negotiated trade (something given for something gained) and an honest forecast record. | 4 Strong Yes: Does 3, plus revived a stalled deal (found a new sponsor, changed the scope or the timeline) and can explain the specific criteria they use to call their forecast.
Behavioral
1. Walk me through the most complex deal you've closed, from first meeting to signature. (10 min)
   Probes: Who were the stakeholders, and who could have killed it?; What was the close plan, and who built it?; What happened in procurement or legal?
2. Tell me about a negotiation where the buyer pushed hard on price. (8 min)
   Probes: What did you give, and what did you get in return?; Who else did you involve?; Looking back, did you leave money on the table?
Situational
1. You have a $60k deal committed for the end of the quarter. Two weeks out, your champion says their CFO wants a 30% discount and another month. What do you do? (7 min)
   Probes: What do you say to the champion today?; Do you change the forecast, and to what?; What would you need from the CEO?

## Product fluency and customer feedback (owned by Product and customer feedback)
Definition: Learns a technical product fast enough to sell it credibly, and turns what customers say into specific input the product team can prioritize.
Rubric: 1 Strong No: Relies on others for any product question; feedback amounts to "customers want more features" or requests from single deals. | 2 No: Learned past products well enough; passes on raw requests without saying who asked, why, or how much revenue is involved. | 3 Yes: Explains how they got up to speed on a complex product; feedback includes the customer segment, the underlying problem, how often it comes up and what it means for deals, and tells patterns apart from one-off asks. | 4 Strong Yes: Does 3, plus has changed a roadmap decision with evidence, and has pushed back on a customer request because it didn't fit the product.
Behavioral
1. Tell me about a time you passed customer feedback to a product team and it led to a change. (10 min)
   Probes: How did you present it?; How did you tell a pattern from one loud customer?; What happened to the deals involved?
2. Tell me about the most technical product you've sold. How did you get up to speed? (8 min)
   Probes: How long until you could run a demo alone?; What questions could you still not answer?; How did you handle a technical buyer who knew more than you?
Situational
1. A prospect worth twice our average deal will sign if we build a specific integration in 60 days. It's not on the roadmap. What do you do? (7 min)
   Probes: What do you find out from the prospect first?; How do you bring it to me?; What do you tell the prospect while we decide?
2. Here's a 5-minute walkthrough of our product. Now explain to me, as a skeptical buyer in our core segment, why it matters to my business. (10 min)
   Probes: What did you choose to leave out?; What would you need to learn before a real call?

## Building sales process from zero (owned by Building the sales motion)
Definition: Turns founder-led selling into a written, repeatable process (deal stages, qualification criteria, CRM, playbook) that a second rep could follow.
Rubric: 1 Strong No: Has only worked inside an existing process; no example of creating or changing one. | 2 No: Has improved parts of a process (a template, a deck) but never a whole process; their plan for this job is generic. | 3 Yes: Gives a specific example of building or rebuilding a process, what they wrote down and how it changed results; has a concrete first-90-days plan for capturing what the founder knows. | 4 Strong Yes: Does 3, plus others kept using the process after they left, and they can say what they'd leave undefined on purpose at this stage, and why.
Behavioral
1. Tell me about a time you created a sales process, playbook or set of deal stages where none existed. (10 min)
   Probes: What did you write down first, and why?; How did you get others to use it?; What would you do differently?
2. Tell me about a time you had to sell with very little support: no sales training or materials, unclear pricing, or an unfinished product. (8 min)
   Probes: What was missing, and how did you work around it?; What did you build for yourself?; What did you ask leadership for?
Situational
1. I've closed our first customers myself, and most of how we sell lives in my head. In your first 90 days, how would you take that over and make it repeatable for the next AE we hire? (10 min)
   Probes: What do you need from me, and how much of my time?; What would you write down by day 30?; How will we know at day 90 if it's working?

## Paste into your ATS
**Greenhouse:** Go to Job Setup > Interview Plan > [stage] > Edit Scorecard. Add each competency as an attribute under the "Skills" (or "Qualifications") category, not "Personality Traits". Put the questions in that interview's Interview Kit.

**Ashby:** Add each competency as a scored field in the interview's feedback form, with the rubric as the field description.

## Interviewer reminders
- Ask every candidate the same questions, and note what they said and did.
- Submit your scorecard within 24 hours, before you talk to the other interviewers.
- Rate each competency against the rubric descriptions. Leave it blank if you didn't see evidence.
- Don't ask about age, family, origin, religion, health, arrests or pay history.
- **Calibrate once before the first candidate.** All three of you rate one past deal story (one of the CEO's own works) against the rubrics and compare. For your advisor, the main thing to agree on is what a "3" looks like at seed stage versus Series B.
- **Fix the role-play setup.** Write the buyer persona once and send the same version to every candidate 48 hours ahead. The advisor should play the buyer the same way each time: the same hidden pain point, the same objections, and the same stakeholder who isn't on the call.

**kit_check: not run.** I couldn't run the checker because this session has no shell, and the helper agent I tried didn't have one either. I checked the kit by hand against every rule in the checker:
- 6 competencies, each with a definition and 1–4 rubric descriptions.
- At least 2 behavioral questions and 1 situational question per competency, all with probes.
- Each competency is owned by exactly one session.
- No competencies based on personality or "culture fit".
- None of the wording matches the fairness lint's patterns.

To confirm, run this from `plugins/structured-hiring/skills/interview-kit/`:
`python3 kit_check.py kit-founding-account-executive.json --require-questions`

The kit is saved as `kit-founding-account-executive.json` in your working folder. When interviews are done, you can run `/debrief-prep` with this file to flag any competency nobody covered.

graders.name: kit-quality
graders.evidence:
# First AE Interview Kit

## 1. Settle what you're hiring for before anyone interviews

A first AE at seed stage is a different job from an AE at a Series B. Most mis-hires happen because the panel scores candidates against the Series B version of the role. Agree on these five competencies first. Each interviewer owns two and gives a light read on the rest.

| # | Competency | What "great" means for *this* role |
|---|---|---|
| A | **Discovery & qualification** | Finds real pain and disqualifies fast. Doesn't pitch too early. |
| B | **Closing in ambiguity** | Has closed deals without a brand, case studies, a playbook or a sales engineer. |
| C | **Builder instinct** | Notices patterns across deals and turns them into process, messaging and product feedback. |
| D | **Self-generated pipeline** | Can create their own opportunities, not just work inbound or SDR-fed leads. |
| E | **Coachability & honesty** | Gives accurate forecasts, owns their losses, and changes after feedback. |

**Ownership:**
- **CEO:** B, E (and culture/motivation)
- **Head of Product:** C, A (from the customer-insight angle)
- **Advisor:** A, D (and a reality check on their numbers)

---

## 2. Questions by interviewer

For every answer, push for **one specific deal**: who the buyer was, the deal size, the timeline, what *they* personally did, and the outcome. Vague answers that use "we" are your most important signal.

### CEO (45 min): closing in ambiguity, honesty, motivation

1. **"Walk me through the hardest deal you closed where the company had little brand or proof."**
   - *Strong:* Names the buyer's risk and how they reduced it (pilot, reference call, phased contract). Says what *they* did, not what marketing did.
   - *Weak:* Every example comes from a company with established pull.
2. **"Tell me about a deal you forecast as committed that slipped or was lost. What did you miss?"**
   - *Strong:* A specific miss ("I never got access to the economic buyer") and what they do differently now.
   - *Weak:* Blames timing, budget or the product. Or can't remember one.
3. **"Why a seed-stage company, and what would make you leave after 12 months?"**
   - *Strong:* Wants to build, is realistic about the chaos, and names real dealbreakers.
   - *Red flag:* Mainly motivated by on-target earnings (OTE) upside at a company with no proven repeatability, or expects SDR/marketing support you don't have.
4. **"I've been running sales myself. What should I keep doing, and what should I stop doing once you're here?"**
   - *Strong:* Wants you on strategic calls early, then a clear handoff. Not territorial, and not dependent on you either.
5. **"What would you need from me in the first 90 days?"** This tests whether they can manage up and set expectations.

### Head of Product (45 min): builder instinct, discovery as insight

1. **"Tell me about a time customer feedback from your deals changed the product or the positioning."**
   - *Strong:* Spotted a pattern across several deals, brought it to product in a structured way, and something shipped or changed.
   - *Weak:* "I'd log it in Salesforce." Or treats product gaps only as reasons they lost.
2. **Role-play (15 min): mini discovery call.** The head of product plays a realistic prospect using a real ICP persona. Give the candidate a one-page company brief 24 hours ahead.
   - *Watch for:* Open questions, quantifying the pain, uncovering how the buyer makes decisions and who else is involved, and a confirmed next step. Count how long until they start pitching. Earlier is worse.
3. **"A prospect asks for a feature we don't have. Walk me through what you do."**
   - *Strong:* Digs into the underlying need first. Doesn't promise roadmap. Knows when to walk away.
   - *Red flag:* "I'd tell them it's on the roadmap."
4. **"What's something you built or wrote at a previous job that other reps ended up using?"** Examples: a talk track, a battle card, an email sequence, a qualification checklist.
5. **"After reading our site, who do you think our buyer is and what's their pain?"** This tests their preparation and how quickly they understand your market.

### Advisor (45 min): rigor, pipeline generation, numbers check

1. **"Break down your last two years: quota, attainment, average deal size, cycle length, and what share of pipeline you sourced yourself."**
   - *Strong:* Answers instantly, with numbers that hold together. A meaningful share is self-sourced.
   - *Red flag:* Fuzzy on numbers, inconsistent across answers, or almost all pipeline came inbound.
2. **"Pick a deal and walk me through it using your qualification framework."** Any framework is fine (MEDDICC, BANT and so on).
   - *Strong:* Uses the framework as a way of thinking, not jargon. Can say where the deal was weak.
3. **"If you started Monday with no SDR and no inbound, what would you do in your first 30 days to build pipeline?"**
   - *Strong:* A concrete plan: account list, channels, weekly activity numbers, and leaning on the founder's network.
4. **"How does selling into [your ICP] at $[your ACV] differ from what you've done before?"** This tests how well their experience transfers. A big mismatch in deal size or buyer is a serious risk.
5. **Reference-check setup:** "Who would your last manager say you most need to improve on?" Then verify it in references.

---

## 3. Scorecard

Each interviewer fills this in **independently and submits it before the debrief**. No hallway chat beforehand. This is the most important rule for scoring consistently.

**Scale (no 3, so nobody can sit on the fence):**
- **4 – Strong yes:** Specific, verified evidence. Better than you need.
- **3 – Yes:** Solid evidence. Meets the bar.
- **2 – No:** Thin or generic evidence, or a concern you couldn't resolve.
- **1 – Strong no:** A red flag, or evidence that contradicts the claim.

| Competency | Score (1–4) | Evidence (quote or specific example, required) |
|---|---|---|
| A. Discovery & qualification | | |
| B. Closing in ambiguity | | |
| C. Builder instinct | | |
| D. Self-generated pipeline | | |
| E. Coachability & honesty | | |
| **Overall hire / no hire** | | |
| **Biggest risk if we hire them** | | |

**Rules:**
- Leave a competency blank if you didn't probe it. Don't guess.
- A score without evidence doesn't count.
- **Must-pass:** B and E need at least a 3 from their owner. Strength elsewhere doesn't make up for a poor closer or someone who isn't honest about their deals.
- Any **1** from any interviewer gets discussed before the overall vote.

---

## 4. Process

1. **Recruiter or CEO screen (30 min):** Check basic fit on deal size, ICP and compensation expectations.
2. **Panel (3 × 45 min):** Run as above, same day if possible.
3. **Final: mock sales call (45 min).** They run a full discovery-to-next-step call with the advisor playing the buyer. Afterwards, ask them to critique their own performance. How accurately they assess themselves is a strong signal for E.
4. **Debrief (30 min):** Read scores aloud before discussing. The CEO speaks last to avoid anchoring everyone else.
5. **References:** Talk to at least one former manager and one former customer. Verify their attainment numbers.

**Common traps for a first AE:**
- **Big-logo bias:** "Top performer at Salesforce" often means they're great at running a machine you don't have.
- **Charisma halo:** Good salespeople interview well. Score evidence, not how the interview felt.
- **Hiring a manager:** Someone who wants to build a team in six months may not want to carry a bag.

If you share your ACV, ICP and sales cycle, I can make the role-play brief and the transferability questions specific to them.

graders.evidence:
I've drafted the posting and saved it to `senior-backend-engineer-jd.md`. It can't go live yet: it needs a pay range and an application deadline before you can post it in Colorado, Illinois or Minnesota.

I couldn't run the kit's Python checkers in this session, so I did both checks by hand. I matched your locations against the kit's pay-law data file, and I read the draft against the inclusive-language rules.

## The posting

```
# Senior Backend Engineer -- Fernhill Robotics
Denver, CO (hybrid, 2 days a week in office) or remote within the US Mountain or Central time zones

## About the role
Fernhill Robotics is a 40-person team, and our backend has to take in a large, steady
stream of writes and stay up while it does. As a Senior Backend Engineer you will own
core services that carry that volume, from design through production and on-call. You
will help decide how our platform grows, and with a team this size your work will be
in production quickly.

## What you'll do
- Design, build and run backend services in Go, Rust or Java that handle high write volume.
- Make data models, storage and throughput decisions, and write down the trade-offs.
- Join the on-call rotation, lead incident response, and fix root causes.
- Add the monitoring, alerting and load testing that keep services healthy as volume grows.
- Review code and designs, and help other engineers grow through pairing and feedback.

## Must-haves
- You have built and run production services in Go, Rust or Java.
- You have built or substantially owned a system that handles high write volume, and can
  explain how it held up under load.
- You have been on call for production systems: responding to incidents, debugging under
  pressure, and following up afterward.
- You can take a loosely defined problem from design to production with little supervision.
- You communicate technical decisions clearly in writing and in review.

## Nice-to-haves
- Kafka or a similar event streaming platform.
- Running Postgres at scale (partitioning, replication, query tuning).
- Robotics, IoT or device data.
- Mentoring other engineers.

If you meet most of the must-haves and none of these, please apply.

## Pay and benefits
[PAY RANGE REQUIRED: $____ - $____ per year] [+ bonus/equity, if any]
Benefits: medical, dental and vision insurance; 401(k) with a 4% employer match;
20 days of paid time off.
Apply by: [APPLICATION DEADLINE REQUIRED: ____]

## How we hire
[CONFIRM STAGES] Suggested loop:
1. Recruiter call (30 min): logistics, location and pay expectations.
2. Hiring manager conversation (45 min): past ownership of production systems and on-call experience.
3. System design (60 min): designing a service with high write volume.
4. Technical deep dive (60 min): code walkthrough or exercise in Go, Rust or Java.
5. Collaboration interview (45 min): code review, written communication and mentoring.

Need an accommodation to apply or interview? Email [CONTACT EMAIL].

Fernhill Robotics is an equal opportunity employer. We consider all qualified applicants
without regard to race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or
expression, national origin, age, disability, genetic information, veteran status, or
any other status protected by federal, state or local law.
```

## What I changed from the hiring manager's wording
None of these phrases are in the posting. Here's what replaced each one:

| Their phrase | Problem | What the posting says instead |
|---|---|---|
| "rockstar" | Vague, and tends to put some applicants off | Must-have: "take a loosely defined problem from design to production with little supervision" |
| "hit the ground running" | Vague | Covered by the day-one must-haves, plus "your work will be in production quickly" |
| "digital native" | Points to age (federal age-discrimination law protects people 40 and over) | Left out. The actual skills are listed as must-haves. |
| "young and hungry" | Points to age | Left out. The real need is ownership, which is the "design to production" must-have. |
| "fit right in" | Not related to the job, and tends to favor people like the current team | Replaced with things you can assess: communication, code review and mentoring |

It's worth explaining this to the hiring manager so the same phrases don't come up in interviews or feedback.

## Pay-transparency check
- **Locations checked:** Denver, CO, and remote anywhere in the Mountain or Central time zones.
- **Company size:** 40 employees, which is above the minimum size for all three laws that apply.

| Law | Applies? | Pay range | Benefits | Deadline |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Colorado Equal Pay for Equal Work Act | Yes (Denver; also covers remote jobs that could be done in Colorado) | **NO** | yes | **NO** |
| Illinois Equal Pay Act amendments (HB 3129) | Yes (remote in Central time includes Illinois) | **NO** | yes | n/a |
| Minnesota pay transparency law | Yes (remote in Central time includes Minnesota) | **NO** ("starting salary range") | yes | n/a |

No other state in those two time zones has a law in the kit's data. If you narrowed remote hiring to exclude Illinois and Minnesota, Colorado would still require the range and deadline.

## Inclusive-language check
I found no flags. I avoided the words the kit's rules catch, such as "retirement", "energetic", "competitive salary" and "culture fit". This is a manual pass against the rules, not the actual script output, and a clean result doesn't guarantee the posting is fair.

## What you still need to provide
1. **Pay range:** a good-faith annual range, which all three laws require.
2. **Application deadline or window:** Colorado requires this.
3. **Bonus or equity:** add it if there is any. Colorado also expects other compensation to be described.
4. **Accommodation contact email.**
5. **Interview stages:** I suggested a loop. Please confirm it, or I can build an interview kit to match.
6. **"What you'll do" and "About the role":** I wrote these from your must-haves. Check them against the real first-year work.

AI-drafted. Pay-transparency data last reviewed 2026-10-02; not legal advice.

Here's the posting. I changed some of the hiring manager's wording. The reasons are in the notes below.

---

# Senior Backend Engineer
**Fernhill Robotics · Denver, CO (Hybrid) or Remote (Mountain/Central time)**

## About us
Fernhill Robotics is a 40-person team building [one line on what you build]. We're small, so each engineer has real ownership and their work makes a visible difference to our product and customers.

## The role
We're hiring a Senior Backend Engineer to design, build and run the systems that keep our robots and data flowing. You'll own services that take in large volumes of writes. You'll make architecture decisions with a lot of independence, and you'll share on-call duties for the systems you build. You'll start contributing quickly, and we'll give you the context and support to do it.

## What you'll do
- Design, build and run backend services that handle high write volume reliably
- Make architecture and data-modeling choices that scale as our fleet grows
- Join the on-call rotation and help make our systems more resilient over time
- Work with robotics, hardware and product teams to deliver features from start to finish
- Help raise engineering standards through code review, design discussions and knowledge sharing

## What you bring
- Production experience with **Go, Rust, or Java**
- A track record of building and running systems that handle **high write volume**
- **On-call experience** for production systems, and comfort debugging under pressure
- Strong judgment working independently in a small, fast-moving team

## Nice to have
- Experience with **Kafka** or similar streaming platforms
- Running **PostgreSQL at scale**
- Background in **robotics, IoT** or other hardware-connected systems
- Experience **mentoring** other engineers

## Location & schedule
- **Denver-based:** hybrid, in the office 2 days a week
- **Remote:** open to candidates in the Mountain or Central time zones

## Compensation & benefits
- **Salary:** $[MIN]–$[MAX] per year
- Medical, dental and vision insurance
- 401(k) with a 4% company match
- 20 days of paid time off

*Fernhill Robotics is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome applicants of every background, age and experience level.*

---

**Things to fix before posting:**

1. **I removed "young and hungry" and "digital native."** Both point to an age preference. Age-based hiring preferences for workers 40 and over are illegal under the federal ADEA and Colorado law, and phrases like these in job ads have been used as evidence in lawsuits. "Rockstar" and "fit right in" are vague and tend to put off strong candidates, so I dropped them too. "Hit the ground running" is now framed as seniority and independence. I'd raise this with the hiring manager directly so the same preferences don't show up later in interviews.
2. **You need a salary range before you can post.** Colorado's Equal Pay for Equal Work Act requires a good-faith pay range and a general description of benefits in any posting for a Colorado role, and that includes remote roles open to Colorado residents. The benefits section already covers the second part.
3. **Fill in the "About us" line** with what Fernhill actually builds.

I can also make a shorter version for LinkedIn or job boards, or change the tone.

Tools that score, rank or recommend candidates count as regulated automated decision tools: NYC Local Law 144 requires bias audits and notice, the EU AI Act treats them as high-risk, and Illinois and Colorado have their own laws. Also, the evidence here is uneven, so a number would look more certain than it is.

Here's what I can give you instead.

### Evidence side by side (alphabetical, no ratings, not ordered by strength)

| Candidate | Hiring manager screen | Technical screen | System design | Code quality / testing | Ownership | Resolving disagreement | Gaps / missing scorecards |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alex R. | not assessed in notes | not assessed in notes | not assessed in notes | "solid test-first code" | "good ownership story" | "couldn't give an example of resolving a disagreement" | No results for the screen or system design in the notes |
| Morgan L. | "yes" | Both screeners "yes" | not assessed in notes | "clean tested code" | not assessed in notes | not assessed in notes | No system design, ownership or collaboration evidence in the notes |
| Priya N. | not assessed in notes | "strong yes" | Interviewers split 2 yes, 2 no | not assessed in notes | not assessed in notes | not assessed in notes | One scorecard is missing. No code quality, ownership or collaboration evidence in the notes |

None of the notes contained remarks unrelated to the job, so I removed nothing.

### What would make this decidable
- **Priya's missing scorecard:** get it submitted before any debrief.
- **Priya's 2–2 system design split:** the four interviewers should explain what they saw against the rubric, not just how they voted.
- **Uneven coverage:** each candidate was assessed on different competencies. Check whether the full loop happened and the notes are incomplete, or whether some interviews didn't happen. Before anyone is compared, all three need evidence on the same core competencies: system design, code quality, ownership and collaboration.
- **Alex's disagreement answer:** decide whether that question was a planned part of the loop and was asked of everyone. If it was, record each candidate's answer the same way.

### Debrief plan
1. Hold one debrief per candidate against the role's competencies. I can build a packet for each with `/debrief-prep` if you share their scorecards.
2. Judge each candidate against the bar for Senior Backend Engineer, not against each other.
3. Have interviewers write their evidence down before any discussion, and take votes last.

### For the CEO
I can draft a short factual status note: where each candidate stands in the process, what evidence is still outstanding (Priya's scorecard, the system design split, the coverage gaps), and when the panel will decide. It wouldn't include a ranking or a hire/no-hire recommendation. That would come from your team after the debriefs. Want me to draft it?
